The shooter that Tencent abandoned: Wardogs hits 2m sales in one weekend
“For six years, we’ve made redundancies every year. This will be the first time we haven’t”
Christopher Dring
Sep 15, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Bulkhead’s Joe Brammer on…
The surprise success of Wardogs
The realities of crunch
Being clear, not transparent
The FPS Games Show, and more
In December last year, Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer warned his 100-person team they faced redundancy.
The UK studio, best known for the military first-person shooter Battalion 1944 , had been owned by Tencent. But the Chinese giant no-longer wanted it. Brammer was working on a deal with investment group Hiro Capital and Team17 parent Everplay, but there was no guarantee of success.
So Brammer advised his team: if you can find a new job, take it.
“What happened was the whole team went, ‘Joe, we’ve got your back, you can do this’,” Brammer shares on today’s episode of The Game Business Show.
“And I’m there like, ‘I can’t do this! Take the job! I’m telling you we’re going down!’ It was a great team moment and they stuck together, but if we hadn’t pulled it off, I would have been like, ‘Guys, please’.”
The money did come in, but the situation was still precarious. Its longer-term survival rested on its 100-player tactical first-person shooter Wardogs. Under Tencent, the game was planned as a significant AAA title, but now it needed scaling back with an Early Access approach. The “bare minimum” it needed to sell was 400,000 copies. Bulkhead would still need to make some redundancies, and take on co-dev projects, but it would survive. If it could sell 600,000 units, that would have been ‘okay’.
Wardogs sold one million copies in pre-orders alone. That number has now surpassed two million.
“We haven’t had much time to celebrate,” he says.
“It was obviously a lot bigger than we expected. Which is great, it’s also been: ‘Oh my God.’ Like DDoS attacks, constant cheaters, and things that, at scale, are just bigger problems.”
Bulkhead now face the good challenge of trying to work out how to deal with this success. It will mean hiring more people, but Brammer is wary having overseen six years of continued layoffs.
“For the last six years, we have made redundancies every single year, about 20% of the company. This will be the first year we haven’t done it,” he reveals.
“We’re very conscious of scaling up and upheaving people’s lives, and also getting a stain for doing this. We want to lean more and more into the gig economy approach. What we’ve been doing is going, ‘You’re really good. We want you to leave your job and come work with us. Why don’t you do 12 or 18 months remote? And if we get along, we’ll give you a big load of money in a fixed offer to come and work for us in-office’.”
“We definitely need to scale. But we need people, and the cost of co-dev is so high and the reliability is so low, the best way for us to do it is to hire internally. So, we’re trying to rush, and people who like FPS games are who we’re looking for.”
“Wardogs is closer to Meccha Chameleon than it is to Call of Duty”
That’s what Brammer believes is key to Wardogs success. The first-person shooter genre may seem impenetrable from the outside. But if you have a team that loves the genre, then it’s possible to break in.
“Very few people make a game like Battalion 1944 and the game bombs, I mean it made some money and got us on the map, right? But it bombs. And then you go, ‘Let’s try that again, but bigger.’ No one does that.
“It’s very penetrable, but to pretend you can be an analyst wanting to get into FPS games is a mistake. You have to be an FPS player, because the community is so vicious and fragmented. I’ve said this a couple of times to people: Wardogs is closer to Meccha Chameleon than it is to Call of Duty. When we were designing Wardogs, it was about the social aspects. If you look at men 18 to 40-years-old, there’s a lot of lonely, bored, or underappreciated men who miss their mates. Wardogs’ audience is 99.9% male. That doesn’t mean we don’t want women playing the game. But we realized we needed to provide a space for them to have fun and do silly things, a space where a 35-year-old man can still make a penis joke. That’s kind of what it is.”
It’s certainly found its audience. And with two million sales in one weekend, you’d have to imagine Tencent is feeling a sense of regret.
“We had a great time with Tencent, and this game wouldn’t be possible without them,” Brammer tells us. “There are people at lots of the companies we’ve worked with over the years, as far back as Square Enix - they were our first publisher - I think everyone like that is kicking themselves.
“Tencent has got plenty of good things coming. But with Wardogs, they pushed us really hard to make something great.”

“We’re not transparent, and we’re not honest”
With the technical problems, Brammer advised dissatisfied players to get a refund and then return once the issues are solved. It’s somewhat in keeping with Bulkhead’s brand, the firm even put out a marketing video before launch listing 10 reasons not to buy the game.
I asked about this level of transparency and honesty, but Brammer insists that’s not what they’re doing.
“ We’re not transparent, and we’re not honest. We’re being clear. Right now, it’s in our interest to be transparent about some things, but we’re not telling everyone everything we’re doing. The brand is becoming that they believe we’re transparent and honest. That’s creating a new problem in that if we choose not to be transparent or honest about something, therefore we’re moving away from the thing that people believe we are.
“We’ve always been the same. My LinkedIn is famously divisive. There was something from Satya Nadella where he said ‘people should know what a leader stands for’. People know what I believe. They know I don’t believe in work-from-home for making video games. They know I expect people to crunch. I own that. I don’t try and hide it.”
He continues: “We knew that ‘10 Reasons Why’ video, when we wrote it, was a hit. But in many ways, it was obvious to us. It’s obviously not Call of Duty. Don’t buy us if you want to play Call of Duty. So, just saying it and owning it in all aspects of Bulkhead and Wardogs’ marketing has been the way to go. But I wouldn’t necessarily call it honest and transparent.”
That clarity can be helpful in business as much as it helps with players.
“We know what we want to make. This was the problem from Square Enix up to Tencent, Splash Damage, and even Team17, to some degree. Through each layer we’ve gone through, we’ve got tougher, saying, ‘We don’t want to listen to you.’ Sometimes that makes enemies. But what we’ve found it’s usually the middle management layer that seems to really struggle with having their position threatened. The higher-up people seem to really like our approach: ‘We know what we’re making. If you don’t like it, don’t fund it’.”
The FPS Games Show was ‘harder than we thought’
Wardogs didn’t make it into Gamescom Opening Night Live, and so Bulkhead decided to do its own showcase dedicated to shooters. The aptly titled: FPS Games Show.
“[It went] better than we thought,” Brammer says.
“It was really cool that we could make something specific and bespoke for that audience. To be clear, I’d love Geoff to come in and take this over, because it was harder than I thought. And he’d do a better job.
“Our very public and unfair feedback to big shows is that I don’t want my big game to be next to an Asian MMO, because it’s my big opportunity and you just get mixed messaging. Then the players dogpile something, but they never should have even been watching it. But we wanted to be in those big ones, right? There’s a prestige that goes with it that the FPS Game Show will never deliver.
“We want to do more of a festival-type thing going forward and to have some sort of paid tier, because it did cost us a fair bit, but really just covering costs. And then having a pre-show, a bit like an opening act, where for free you can put those teams of 1 to 10 people making neat FPS games. We’re toying with different ideas at the moment.”
“We always try and avoid crunch, but it’s going to happen”
Brammer is open about the fact that he expects his team to crunch when the time comes. He compares the situation to a balancing act, but one where things shift from one extreme to the other.
“For the last three months, Wardogs has been more important than a lot of [our team’s] family lives,” Brammer says. “But now, Bulkhead and I have to acknowledge that it needs to go the other way. Everyone’s pushing us to get console out earlier, and we’ve said, ‘No, that’s not how it’s going to work. We can’t push them more. We’re not doing that. It’s going to release in 2028’.”
The company will be getting the whole of December off, Brammer adds.
His perspective on crunch is undoubtedly controversial, but he says he’s upfront about it. It’s not something a new recruit is going to discover after joining.
“A lot of people who may have an issue with crunch - rightly so, I understand that issue, we always try and avoid it, but we don’t hide that this is going to happen at some point - they often don’t make it in the door,” he says. “We want to be known for that: this is a place you come to work hard. If you care about the work you’re making and the result of what you make here, you’ll feel really valued. If you don’t, you will feel slave-driven. We check people’s socials, and if you’re constantly tweeting anti-crunch messaging: ‘This should never ever be a thing’, we know that and go, ‘Look, you’re not going to be happy here, so we’re not going to go with you’.”
The upside to working like this, Brammer says, is the financial reward. Not everyone within Bulkhead owns shares or receives bonuses, but those that do get a meaningful amount.
“If we’re going to be a company who says, ‘We do crunch’, then we have to also say, ‘But you get something for it.’ We want people to know that those people who do work hard get that return, and it is life-changing.
He concludes: “I’m going to be really excited to see juniors who have been with us for two or three years who are going to get money to buy a house, or at least a down payment. What we actually find is we have to coach them.... please don’t spend all your money on takeaway and energy drinks. We have a new responsibility to our younger staff who are making good money, often money they haven’t seen before.”

title: Sensor Tower 2026年8月全球手游收入与下载量排行榜 TOP 10
text:
根据 Sensor Tower 应用表现洞察最新数据，《 王者荣耀 》在8月继续领跑全球手游收入榜。在中国市场，游戏于8月8日至15日期间推出“夏日农友节”和“无尽之局平行世界”两大重磅活动。此次更新不仅推出了新英雄“卢雅那”，还上线限时玩法“超极限狂潮”，通过缩短技能冷却时间、提供可叠加升级效果，并配合免费抽奖、全新外观及活动专属奖励，通过多样化玩法与奖励机制持续刺激玩家参与和付费。
《 Gossip Harbor 》在8月同样展现出亮眼表现，这主要得益于其节奏合理的运营活动规划。“Water Wonders（水上奇观）”和“Dollhouse of Dreams（梦幻娃娃屋）”将7月积累的热度延续至8月上半月；随后推出的“四周年庆典（Fourth-Year Festivities）”围绕周年主题设置合成任务和专属奖励，进一步丰富了游戏内容。进入8月下旬，龙族救援剧情活动“Slay the Dragon, Save the Day!（屠龙救援行动）”继续吸引玩家参与；“Escape from Raccoon Beach（逃离浣熊海滩）”和秋季主题活动“The Turning Leaves（秋叶流转）”则带来新的收集任务，并将活动延续至9月。
其他头部收入产品同样依靠持续推出的主题活动维持用户参与度与付费意愿。《 Whiteout Survival 》在8月推出内容丰富的活动矩阵，其中与《Kingshot》的联动成为当月重点。核心活动“Twin Star Adventure（双星历险记）”以北极熊探险为主题，结合了剧情和合作玩法；“State of Power（最强王国）”和“Winter Siege（冬日攻城战）”等联盟竞赛，则让玩家持续参与团队竞争。《 Royal Match 》于8月推出“Dragon Nest（龙之巢穴）”以及限时竞赛“Lightning Rush（闪电冲刺）”，进一步丰富了合作与竞技玩法。《 Candy Crush Saga 》则通过节奏有序的内容更新维持玩家热度，先后推出“Bubblegum Season（泡泡糖赛季）”、多轮赛事“Candy Cup 2026（糖果杯2026）”，并在8月底上线“Music Season（音乐赛季）”。
完整手游收入 TOP 10 榜单请参见上图。注：本文数据不包含第三方安卓渠道。
2026年8月，全球玩家在 App Store 和 Google Play 上的移动游戏支出达到65.7亿美元，环比下降1%。在市场份额方面，美国以28.6%的总收入占比继续保持全球领跑地位；中国（仅统计 iOS 端）以16.7%紧随其后；日本则以12.2%位列第3。
在全球手游收入增长榜中，回合制 RPG《 Fate/Grand Order 》位居第1名。其增长主要由日本市场推动，游戏在8月创下2026年以来的单月收入新高。11周年庆典为玩家带来每日登录奖励、全新任务、特别挑战以及以新角色“阿兹拉伊勒的哈桑”为核心的限时卡池。随后上线的年度“泳装活动2026”进一步推出夏日主题外观与全新可收集角色，推动玩家付费热度延续至9月初。
在8月全球手游收入增长榜前十名中，腾讯旗下或由腾讯发行的产品占据五席。其中，《 金铲铲之战（Teamfight Tactics） 》和《 无畏契约（VALORANT） 》分别位列第2名和第3名，增长主要来自中国市场。《金铲铲之战》推出全新“自然之力”赛季，带来新的角色和策略选择，并同步上线可自由切换双形态的卓越级英雄“不朽格温”。《无畏契约》则在手游上线一周年之际推出两套主题武器系列，分别是融入中国传统艺术元素的“墨武（Ink Warrior）”以及以花卉为设计主题的“千灵华绽（Thousand Spirits）”。
《 和平精英（Game for Peace） 》、《 英雄联盟手游（League of Legends: Wild Rift） 》和《 三角洲行动（Delta Force） 》同样实现榜单排名上升。《和平精英》推出来自国产动画《吞噬星空》的联动角色、武器与载具；《英雄联盟手游》将四周年庆典奖励与全新“水晶玫瑰2026”系列角色皮肤相结合；《三角洲行动》则通过“宝藏月”活动鼓励玩家持续登录、完成对局并搜寻高价值游戏藏品。这些活动表明，腾讯通过重磅版本更新、周年庆典、热门娱乐 IP 联动以及限定外观，为玩家创造持续回流和付费的动力。
新作《 Zeus: The God of Arrogance 》位列全球手游收入增长榜第10名。自8月下旬上线以来，该作持续稳居韩国手游收入榜榜首。作为 Com2uS Holdings 发行的竞技 MMORPG，游戏通过大规模战斗、职业化作战体系以及面向不同成长阶段玩家的竞技玩法，对希腊神话进行重新演绎。此外，游戏还设有离线成长系统，使角色能够在玩家离线期间继续发展；以制造为核心的职业则可以生产专属道具，为长期成长体系与游戏内经济提供支撑。
总体来看，8月榜单显示，头部手游的商业化越来越依赖持续且有层次的 Live Ops，而非单一大型活动。大型版本、周年庆和 IP 联动负责制造阶段性峰值，高频奖励、限时玩法与外观内容则承担承接热度和延长生命周期的作用。与此同时，快速崛起的新作也证明，定位清晰且时机适当的产品仍有机会在竞争激烈的市场中实现突破。欢迎通过 Sensor Tower 旗下 Playliner 运营活动洞察平台 ，深入了解影响游戏商业化及玩家参与度的运营策略。
2026年8月全球手游下载排行榜 TOP 10
《 ROBLOX 》位居2026年8月全球手游下载榜榜首，《 Free Fire 》排名第2。《 Block Blast! 》、《 Subway Surfers 》和《 Arrow Puzzle: Tap Puzzle Games 》紧随其后，共同跻身全球下载榜前五。
《 ROBLOX 》登顶全球手游下载榜，主要得益于其在8月推出的多元化精选体验。其中既包括 MMORPG《Vesteria》和战术 FPS《TTK》，也包括《Dress to Impress》与《Tower Defense Simulator》的大型版本更新。新上线的《Duck Duck》则进一步为平台补充了社交派对玩法。角色扮演、射击、时尚、策略与休闲等多品类内容的持续更新，不仅拓展了 Roblox 的用户吸引力，也帮助平台维持玩家关注度。
《 Free Fire 》在8月继续稳居全球手游下载榜第2名，延续了7月下旬结束的9周年庆典所带来的增长势头。在相对平静的月初过后，“Scarlet Moon（绯红之月）”于8月下旬在《Free Fire》及《Free Fire MAX》中同步上线，通过全新设计与专属奖励焕新经典收藏内容。游戏的持续强劲表现，反映出其稳定的全球吸引力，以及周年庆典活动所带来的长尾增长效应。
《 Subway Surfers 》在8月全球手游下载榜上环比上升三位，排名第4。“Fantasy Fest（奇幻庆典）”世界巡回更新为游戏带来充满魔法色彩的全新场景、新角色和限时挑战，其中还包括提供收集奖励的开学季活动。8月下旬上线的“Cosmic Crossroads（宇宙十字路口）”则将游戏舞台转移至太空主题环境，并加入全新角色、赛季奖励路线，以及回归的《Among Us》联动。主题地点、收集角色、挑战活动及跨界内容的持续轮换，不仅保持了游戏的新鲜感，也进一步吸引新老玩家参与。
2026年8月，全球手游下载量达到37.6亿次，环比增长1%。在国家与地区方面，印度以6.14亿次下载（占比16.4%）继续领跑全球；美国（7.4%）和巴西（5.8%）分别位列第2和第3位。
开放世界犯罪题材成为8月手游下载市场的一大亮点，两款快速崛起的新作引领了这一趋势。《 Gangstar Mirage City 》位居全球手游下载增长榜第1名，并在8月20日于多个市场上线后跻身全球下载总榜第7名。该作由腾讯旗下 Level Infinite 和 Gameloft 合作推出，玩家可以探索未来都市、自定义载具、建立犯罪帝国，并参与抢劫行动与帮派战斗。《 Gangster Miami RP: Grand City 》则位列下载增长榜第6名，为玩家提供由城市探索、驾驶及犯罪主题任务组成的类似体验。
两款游戏的下载增长主要来自印度、印度尼西亚、巴基斯坦和巴西等市场，这些市场本身拥有庞大的手游用户规模，且近期增长较快。两款新作的崛起也反映出，移动端开放世界犯罪题材仍具较强吸引力。与此同时，备受期待的主机游戏《 Grand Theft Auto VI 》也持续受到关注，进一步凸显了开放世界犯罪题材的市场热度。8月底，Rockstar Games 发布了《 Grand Theft Auto VI 》的加长版预告片，为游戏11月19日发售进一步预热。
新作《 Mystery Dumpling: Unbox ASMR 》位列全球手游下载增长榜第2名，并在8月上线后跻身全球下载总榜第12名。该游戏由 Brocker Bus Studio 发行，是一款将神秘盒拆封、ASMR 互动体验与色彩鲜明的卡通画面相结合的超休闲游戏。该作上线首月下载量超过1,100万次，其中印度尼西亚、巴西和土耳其贡献主要增量。
载具题材游戏在8月同样获得增长动能，《 Bus Fever-Car Jam Escape 》、《 Dear Passengers 》和《 Wheelie Master: Moto Ride 3D 》均进入全球手游下载增长榜前十。三款产品分别围绕巴士分类解谜、客运航空模拟以及摩托车特技驾驶展开，为交通运输题材提供了不同的休闲玩法。它们在印度、印度尼西亚、巴西、墨西哥和土耳其等高下载量市场表现突出，也说明简单易懂的载具玩法依然能够吸引大量玩家。
总体来看，8月全球手游下载榜既体现了成熟头部产品的持久生命力，也展现出新作及成长型产品的快速增长。高频内容更新帮助领先产品持续保持市场曝光，而开放世界犯罪、ASMR、解谜和载具模拟等易于上手的玩法，则在多个高下载量移动游戏市场获得较快增长。
